books.title: Tiny Habits
books.author: BJ Fogg, PhD
books.about: *The Small Changes That Change Everything*: a practical method for changing behavior by starting very small, from the founder of Stanford's Behavior Design Lab. [1,2]
books.authorBio: BJ Fogg, PhD, founded the Behavior Design Lab at Stanford University. [2]

principle.name: Design for low motivation
principle.body: Motivation rises and falls through the day, in what Fogg calls the Motivation Wave. When we're tired, it's the first thing to go. A behavior designed to work on your lowest-energy day is far more likely to happen: make it easy, make it visible, anchor it, and make it feel good. [1,4]

framework.name: The Fogg Behavior Model
framework.intro: A **B**ehavior happens when **M**otivation, **A**bility and a **P**rompt come together at the same moment. To design for a behavior, pull on those three levers. [3]

parts.name: Motivation
parts.tagline: How much you want to do it
parts.what: Your desire to do the behavior. It's real but unreliable, so Fogg advises matching yourself with behaviors you already want rather than trying to manufacture motivation. [1,4]
how: Celebrate right after the behavior so it feels good. Fogg calls that feeling **Shine** [5]
Choose behaviors people already want to do [1]

examples.label: Physical
examples.text: Confetti at the marathon finish line

examples.label: Digital
examples.text: A badge after someone's first contribution

examples.label: Experience
examples.text: Stairs that play a note with every step

parts.name: Ability
parts.tagline: How easy it is to do
parts.what: Fogg's Ability Chain: time, money, physical effort, mental effort and fit with your routine. The weakest link sets how hard the behavior feels. [6]
how: **Make it less hard:** remove the weakest link, or make it the default [6]
**Make it tiny:** use a Starter Step (just the first move) or scale it back to a smaller version [6]

examples.label: Physical
examples.text: Seats in small circles so talking is natural

examples.label: Digital
examples.text: A one-tap poll instead of a blank reply box

examples.label: Experience
examples.text: One-word intros to break the ice

parts.name: Prompt
parts.tagline: What reminds you to do it, right now
parts.what: No behavior happens without a prompt. Fogg names three kinds: **Person** prompts (a feeling or body signal), **Context** prompts (something in your surroundings) and **Action** prompts (a routine you already do). Action prompts, which he calls **Anchors**, are the most reliable. [7,8]
how: **Anchor it:** attach the new behavior right after an existing routine [7]
**Make it visible:** put the cue where it can't be missed [1]

examples.label: Physical
examples.text: A sign on the café door: “Joining the run?”

examples.label: Digital
examples.text: “How do you want to show up today?” right after login

examples.label: Experience
examples.text: Grab a coloured badge, find someone with the same colour

framework.note: Motivation is the least reliable lever. When designing, start with ability and prompts. [1,4]

system.name: The Tiny Design Test
system.intro: Run any idea through five levers drawn from Fogg's model.

steps.name: Make it easy
steps.detail: Shrink the action or lower the stakes. [6]

steps.name: Make it less hard
steps.detail: Remove the weakest link in the Ability Chain. [6]

steps.name: Make it visible
steps.detail: Put context prompts in view. [7]

steps.name: Anchor a prompt
steps.detail: Tie it to something people already do. [7]

steps.name: Celebrate completion
steps.detail: Make finishing feel good straight away. [5]

example.title: Café run club
items: **Easy:** shorten the run from 5 km to 1 km
**Less hard:** a QR code on the door for quick sign-up
**Anchor:** the sign on the exit reminds people as they leave
**Visible:** posters show the start time, route and social fun
**Celebrate:** a big group cheer at the finish

reflect: How will you use this model to shape behavior for the better?
How could you design for joy? For calm? For connection?

steps: Choose one outcome to design for: joy, connection, calm, movement…
Write a Tiny Habits recipe for it: “After I [anchor], I will [tiny behavior].” Then decide how you'll celebrate.
Run the idea through one lever of the Tiny Design Test.
Share your design with someone and ask where they'd still feel friction.

books.inSedi: Add the recipe as a Routine in Timely. The little check sound when you tick it is your celebration.

books.title: Indistractable
books.author: Nir Eyal with Julie Li
books.about: *How to Control Your Attention and Choose Your Life*: a guide to understanding distraction and designing your habits, calendar and surroundings for focus. [1,2,5]
books.authorBio: Nir Eyal writes about the intersection of psychology, technology and business, and is also the author of *Hooked*. [3]

principle.name: Design to hack distraction
principle.body: Eyal's starting point is that distraction is mostly an escape from discomfort, not a technology problem. External triggers then hijack attention unless your environment, tools and rituals are designed on purpose. Distraction isn't fixed by willpower. It's fixed by design. [3,4]

framework.name: The Indistractable Model
framework.intro: **Traction** is any action that pulls you toward what you intend; **distraction** pulls you away. Eyal's model has four parts. [3,4]

parts.name: Master internal triggers
parts.what: Boredom, loneliness, worry and fatigue are what push us to distraction. [3]
how: Notice the feeling and write it down before acting on it [3]
Use the 10-minute rule: wait ten minutes before giving in [3,6]
Surf the urge until it passes, a technique Eyal draws from Jonathan Bricker's research [4]
Reimagine the task to find novelty in it, and reimagine your temperament, since willpower doesn't simply run out [4]

examples.label: Your work

examples.label: Your space

parts.name: Make time for traction
parts.tagline: Plan your values into your calendar
parts.what: You can't call something a distraction unless you know what you meant to do instead. [3]
how: Timebox the week across three domains: **You**, **Relationships** and **Work** [3]
Schedule sync: agree your calendar with the people who depend on your time [4,7]

examples.label: Your work

parts.tagline: Is this trigger serving me, or am I serving it?
parts.what: Pings, dings and interruptions are useful only if they lead to traction. [3]
how: Phone: remove, replace, rearrange and reclaim [3]
Meetings: no agenda, no meeting [7,8]
Group chat: get in and get out, like a sauna [3,9]
Signal focus: a screen sign, or a light-up “concentration crown” like the one Eyal's wife wears [3,10]

**Price pact:** put money at stake [3]
**Identity pact:** see yourself as someone who is indistractable [3]

system.name: Design to Hack Distraction
system.intro: Five steps for designing a focused space, team or day, built on Eyal's model.

steps.name: Identify external triggers
steps.detail: Audit what pulls attention away: physical (layout, clutter, movement), digital (screens, notifications) and social (interruptions, open access). [3]

steps.name: Remove or reduce triggers
steps.detail: Focus zones, minimal setups and blocked distractions. Goal: less cognitive tax. [3]

steps.name: Protect with social structure
steps.detail: Timeboxed focus hours, office hours for questions, no agenda no meeting, and get-in-get-out group chat. Goal: lower interruption cost. [3,7,8]

steps.name: Replace with designed cues
steps.detail: Visual and auditory signals for focus time, like a screen sign or a concentration crown. Goal: channel attention on purpose. [3,10]

steps.name: Reinforce focus
steps.detail: Multichannel multitasking (pair low-attention tasks, like walking while listening) and temptation bundling. Goal: sustained effort. [3,11,12]

example.title: A shared studio
items: **Identify:** foot traffic past the desks, a TV, constant Slack pings
**Remove:** desks turned away from the walkway, TV off until 4 pm
**Protect:** focus mornings, questions at 2 pm office hours
**Cue:** a lamp on means “don't interrupt”
**Reinforce:** walking 1:1s and a shared playlist for admin hour

reflect: What feeling usually comes right before you get distracted?
Which trigger around you is serving someone else's goals, not yours?

steps: Keep a Distraction Tracker for three days: each time you get distracted, note the time and the feeling just before.
Look for patterns: which feelings and triggers come up most?
Pick one fix for the most common one: the 10-minute rule, a removed notification, or a pact.
Timebox next week across You, Relationships and Work.

books.inSedi: Timebox the week in Timely's day view, including blocks for yourself and your people, not just work.

books.title: Atomic Habits
books.author: James Clear
books.about: *An Easy & Proven Way to Build Good Habits & Break Bad Ones*: how tiny changes compound into remarkable results, and how to design the cues, cravings and rewards behind every habit. [1,2]
books.authorBio: James Clear writes about habits, decision-making and continuous improvement at jamesclear.com. [3]

principle.name: Design the system, not the goal
principle.body: Clear argues that goals set direction but systems make progress. You don't rise to the level of your goals; you fall to the level of your systems. Small improvements of about 1% compound over time, even when the results stay invisible for a long while (his Plateau of Latent Potential). [2,4,11]

framework.name: The Four Laws of Behavior Change
framework.intro: Every habit runs through a loop of **cue → craving → response → reward**. Each law shapes one stage. To break a bad habit, invert the law. [2]

parts.name: Make it obvious
parts.what: Habits start with a cue you notice. Make the cue for a good habit unmissable and hide the cues for bad ones. [2]
how: Write an implementation intention: “I will [behavior] at [time] in [location]” [6]
Use the habit stacking formula: “After [current habit], I will [new habit]” [6]
Put the cue in plain sight, like the book on your pillow [2]

examples.label: Your day
examples.text: Running shoes by the door

examples.label: Your work
examples.text: Tomorrow's first task written on a sticky note

examples.label: Your space
examples.text: Fruit on the counter, sweets in a high cupboard

parts.name: Make it attractive
parts.what: The more appealing a habit, the more likely you'll do it. [2]
how: Temptation bundling: only do something you want while doing something you need to [7,12]
Join a group where the behavior you want is normal [2]

examples.label: Your day
examples.text: Favourite podcast only on the treadmill

examples.label: Your work
examples.text: Good coffee only during deep-work blocks

examples.label: Your space

parts.name: Make it easy
parts.what: Reduce the friction between you and the good behavior, and add friction to the bad. [2]
how: The Two-Minute Rule: scale a new habit down to a version that takes under two minutes [8]
Prepare your environment so the next action is ready [2]

examples.label: Your day
examples.text: “Read one page” instead of “read more”

examples.label: Your work
examples.text: Open the doc before you close your laptop

examples.label: Your space
examples.text: Phone charger in the kitchen, not the bedroom

parts.name: Make it satisfying
parts.what: We repeat what feels good right away. [2]
how: Track the habit so progress is visible [9]
Never miss twice: one slip is an accident, two starts a pattern [9]
For bad habits, a habit contract with an accountability partner adds an immediate cost [10]

framework.note: Clear frames habits as votes for an identity. Decide who you want to be, then prove it with small wins. Change works best from identity outward, not outcomes inward. [4]

system.name: The Habit Design Card
system.intro: Run one habit through Clear's tools in order.

steps.name: Score your day
steps.detail: List your daily habits and mark each +, – or = for the person you want to be (Clear's Habits Scorecard). [5]

steps.name: Choose the identity
steps.detail: Finish the sentence: “I'm the kind of person who…” [4]

steps.name: Stack it
steps.detail: After [current habit], I will [new habit]. [6]

steps.name: Shrink it
steps.detail: Cut it to a two-minute starting version. [8]

steps.name: Track it
steps.detail: Mark it daily, and never miss twice. [9]

example.title: Becoming a writer
items: **Score:** scrolling at breakfast is a “–”
**Identity:** I'm someone who writes every day
**Stack:** after I pour my first coffee, I'll open my notebook
**Shrink:** write one sentence
**Track:** a tick on the calendar, and never two blanks in a row

reflect: Which of your current habits are votes for the person you want to become, and which are votes against?
If you only fall to the level of your systems, what does your current system produce?

steps: Do the Habits Scorecard: list everything you do from waking up, and mark each item +, – or =. Don't change anything yet.
Choose one “–” to weaken and one new habit to build.
Write the new habit as a stack: “After I…, I will…”.
Shrink it to two minutes and do it once today.

books.title: Nudge
books.author: Richard H. Thaler and Cass R. Sunstein
books.publisher: Yale University Press (2008); Penguin, *Nudge: The Final Edition* (2021)
books.about: *Improving Decisions About Health, Wealth, and Happiness*: how the way choices are presented shapes what people choose, and how to design those choices so people are better off by their own standards. [1,2]
books.authorBio: Richard H. Thaler won the 2017 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences; Cass R. Sunstein is a legal scholar at Harvard. [2,11]

principle.name: There is no neutral design
principle.body: Someone always decides how options are laid out: what comes first, what's the default, what's easy. Thaler and Sunstein call that person a **choice architect**. Since design always influences the choice, design it on purpose to help people while leaving every option open. They call this **libertarian paternalism**. [2,3] They also contrast **Econs**, the perfectly rational people of economic models, with **Humans**, who think with a fast Automatic System and a slow Reflective System and make predictable mistakes. [2,8]

framework.name: NUDGES
framework.intro: The authors' checklist of choice-architecture tools. Each letter is one lever. [4]

parts.name: iNcentives
parts.what: People respond to incentives they notice. Make the real costs and benefits visible at the moment of choice. [4]
how: Show the cost where the decision happens [4]

parts.name: Understand mappings
parts.what: Help people see how a choice translates into results they care about. [4]

parts.tagline: What happens if you do nothing
parts.what: Defaults are powerful because many people stick with them. Automatic enrolment in retirement savings is the classic case. [2,5] The book also describes Save More Tomorrow, where people commit now to save more from future raises. [2,10]
how: Set the default to the option most people would choose on reflection [2]

system.intro: Use the book's tools as your own choice architect.

books.title: Feel-Good Productivity
books.author: Ali Abdaal
books.about: A case that feeling good is the engine of productivity, not the reward for it, built on research from psychology and neuroscience. [1,2]
books.authorBio: Ali Abdaal trained and worked as a doctor in the UK before building one of YouTube's most-watched channels on productivity. [11]

principle.name: Design for good feelings first
principle.body: Abdaal argues that the discipline-and-pressure approach has it backwards. Positive feelings raise energy, energy makes work easier to start and sustain, and the work then feels better still. So instead of forcing output, change how the work feels. [1,2,3]

framework.name: Energise · Unblock · Sustain
framework.intro: The book is built in three parts: what gives us energy, what blocks us from starting, and what keeps us from burning out. Each chapter ends with small experiments to try. [1,2]

parts.name: Energise
parts.what: Three sources of good feeling. **Play**: bringing lightness and curiosity to a task. **Power**: a sense of confidence, competence and control. **People**: feeling part of something with others. [2,3]
how: Ask of a dull task: what would this look like if it were fun? [3]
Choose a character to play while you work, and allow yourself side quests that follow your curiosity [4,12]
Build a sense of power by teaching what you're learning (the protégé effect) and reframing “I have to” as “I get to” [5,13]
Treat collaborators as comrades and over-communicate [3,4]

examples.label: Your day
examples.text: A playlist and a timer turn chores into a race

examples.label: Your work
examples.text: Explain a new skill to a colleague to lock it in

examples.label: Your space
examples.text: A shared table where people work alongside each other

parts.name: Unblock
parts.what: The three things that stop us starting. Each has its own fix: seek **clarity**, find **courage**, and just **get started**. [2]
how: **Uncertainty:** set NICE goals (Near-term, Input-based, Controllable, Energising) instead of distant outcome goals [2,6]
**Fear:** name the feeling, picture how much it will matter in 10 minutes, 10 months and 10 years, and remember others notice us far less than we think [7]
**Inertia:** commit to just five minutes, cut the friction, and define the very next action [4,5]

examples.label: Your day
examples.text: “Walk 20 minutes after lunch” instead of “get fit”

examples.label: Your work
examples.text: Open the doc and write for five minutes, then decide

examples.label: Your space
examples.text: Leave tomorrow's first task open on the desk tonight

parts.name: Sustain
parts.what: Abdaal describes three kinds of burnout: **overexertion** (doing too much), **depletion** (not refilling), and **misalignment** (doing what doesn't fit you). Each has its own remedy. [2,3]
how: **Conserve:** keep an Energy Investment Portfolio, with a short list of active commitments and a separate list of someday dreams [5,14]
**Recharge:** creative hobbies, time in nature, and real rest with nothing planned [3,4]
**Align:** sketch alternative futures with an Odyssey Plan to check that your work points where you want to go [5]

examples.label: Your day
examples.text: One evening a week with nothing scheduled

examples.label: Your work
examples.text: Cap active projects at five, park the rest

examples.label: Your space
examples.text: A hobby corner that's always ready to use

framework.note: Many of the book's tools come from other researchers, and Abdaal credits them: 10/10/10 from Suzy Welch [8], the spotlight effect from Thomas Gilovich and colleagues [9], and the Odyssey Plan from Bill Burnett and Dave Evans [10].

system.name: The Feel-Good Check
system.intro: A five-question pass to run on any task you've been avoiding, built from the book's three parts.

steps.name: Add energy
steps.detail: Where can you add play, power or people? [2]

steps.name: Name the blocker
steps.detail: Is it uncertainty, fear or inertia? [2]

steps.name: Remove it
steps.detail: A NICE goal, a named fear, or five minutes on the clock. [6,7]

steps.name: Check the tank
steps.detail: Is this overexertion, depletion or misalignment? [2]

steps.name: Run it as an experiment

books.title: Designing Your Work Life
books.author: Bill Burnett and Dave Evans
books.about: *How to Thrive and Change and Find Happiness at Work*: the authors of *Designing Your Life* apply design thinking to the job you already have, before deciding whether to leave. Reissued in 2021 as *Designing Your New Work Life*. [1,2]
books.authorBio: Bill Burnett and Dave Evans teach the Designing Your Life course at Stanford University. [3]

principle.name: Redesign before you resign
principle.body: Most people think the only fix for a bad job is a new one. Burnett and Evans argue that you can almost always make the job you have work better first, by reframing stuck beliefs, running small experiments and accepting “good enough for now” as a base to build on. [1,4,5]

framework.name: Reframe · Mix · Redesign
framework.intro: Three of the book's core tools, in the order we find useful. [1,4]

parts.name: Reframe dysfunctional beliefs
parts.what: A stuck belief keeps you stuck. Turn it into a reframe you can act on, such as moving from feeling like a cog in the machine to seeing yourself as a lever that can move it. [4]
how: Write the belief down, then rewrite it as something you could test this week [4]
Practice “good enough for now”: not forever, just a stable base to improve from [4]

examples.label: Your day
examples.text: “I hate Mondays” → “What would make Monday mornings 10% better?”

examples.label: Your work
examples.text: “Nothing will change here” → “What's one thing I could try?”

examples.label: Your space
examples.text: “My desk is depressing” → “What's one thing I'd add?”

parts.name: The Maker's Mix
parts.what: Money versus meaning is a false choice. Instead, rate three kinds of making: **money-making**, **impact-making** and **expression-making**, and set the balance you want, like faders on a mixing desk. [3,5]
how: Score each from 1 to 100 for your current job, then set your ideal mix [3]
Close gaps with small prototypes, including outside work [3]

examples.label: Your day
examples.text: A creative hobby tops up expression

examples.label: Your work
examples.text: Volunteer for a project with visible impact

examples.label: Your space
examples.text: A side gig that adds income

parts.name: Don't resign, redesign
parts.what: **Reframe and re-enlist** (a new why for the same job), **remodel** (change the role), **relocate** (another role in the company), **reinvent** (retrain inside the company). [7]
how: Try them in that order, from smallest change to largest [7]
If you do leave, practise generative quitting: leave in a way that sets up what's next [6,8]

examples.label: Your day
examples.text: Reframe: the commute becomes podcast-learning time

examples.label: Your work
examples.text: Remodel: trade a task you dread for one you like

examples.label: Your space
examples.text: Relocate: join the team you keep helping anyway

framework.note: The book also uses the ARC of autonomy, relatedness and competence (from self-determination theory) to diagnose what's missing at work. Odyssey Plans and the Good Time Journal come from the authors' earlier book, *Designing Your Life*. [5,9]

system.name: The Good Work Journal
system.intro: This book's version of the Good Time Journal: a short daily log that shows what makes work good for you. [4]

steps.name: Learned
steps.detail: Each day, note something you learned. [4]

steps.name: Initiated
steps.detail: Note something you started or took the lead on. [4]

steps.name: Helped
steps.detail: Note someone you helped. [4]

steps.name: Review weekly
steps.detail: Look for surprises and which category dominates. [4]

steps.name: Boost the gap
steps.detail: Plan one way to grow the missing category, then notice how it feels. [4]

example.title: Three weeks of entries
items: **Learned:** a faster way to build the report
**Initiated:** suggested a Friday demo
**Helped:** walked a new hire through the codebase
**Pattern:** “helped” days were the best days
**Boost:** volunteer to mentor once a week

reflect: What's the one belief about your work that feels most stuck?
If your job were “good enough for now”, what would you build on first?

steps: Write your most stuck belief about work, then reframe it as a question you could test.
Score your Maker's Mix: money, impact and expression from 1 to 100, now and ideally.
Pick the biggest gap and design one small prototype to close it.
Start a Good Work Journal tonight: one line each for learned, initiated and helped.

books.inSedi: Make the reframed question a project in Timely's Planning view, with the prototype as its first task.

books.title: The Art of Gathering
books.author: Priya Parker
books.about: *How We Meet and Why It Matters*: a facilitator's guide to designing gatherings of every kind, from dinners to meetings to funerals, around a clear purpose. [1,2]
books.authorBio: Priya Parker is a facilitator and strategic adviser who helps groups have meaningful conversations. [2]

principle.name: Design for a purpose, not a category
principle.body: “Dinner party”, “meeting” and “birthday” are formats, not reasons. Parker argues that most gatherings disappoint because we copy the format and skip the purpose. A good purpose is specific and even disputable: reasonable people could disagree with it. [2,3]

framework.name: The arc of a gathering
framework.intro: The book follows a gathering from first idea to final goodbye. Five of its moves: [2,4]

parts.name: Decide why
parts.what: A funeral can be to mourn a death or to celebrate a life. Those lead to very different gatherings. Choose. [2,3]
how: Ask why three times until the purpose is something someone could disagree with [2]

examples.label: Physical
examples.text: A dinner “to welcome the new neighbours into the street”

examples.label: Digital
examples.text: A call “to decide, not to update”

examples.label: Experience
examples.text: A birthday “to thank the people who got me through this year”

parts.name: Close doors
parts.what: The guest list is the first test of your purpose. Who to leave out, the size of the group and the venue all shape what can happen. [2]
how: Invite only the people who serve the purpose [2]

examples.label: Physical
examples.text: A room just big enough to feel full

examples.label: Digital
examples.text: Six people on the call, not twenty

examples.label: Experience
examples.text: No plus-ones for a reunion dinner

parts.name: Generous authority
parts.what: Hosts who stay hands-off leave guests unprotected. Use your authority generously: protect guests, connect them, and treat them as equals. [2,4]
how: Introduce people, step in when someone dominates, and set the tone [4]

examples.label: Physical
examples.text: Seating planned so strangers meet

examples.label: Digital
examples.text: The host calls on quiet voices by name

examples.label: Experience
examples.text: Gently cutting off the long speech

parts.name: Pop-up rules
parts.what: Explicit, temporary rules that hold only for this gathering replace unspoken etiquette and let people from different backgrounds play the same game. [4]
how: Set two or three simple rules, like no phones or no job titles [4]

examples.label: Physical
examples.text: Phones in a basket at the door

examples.label: Digital
examples.text: Cameras on, no multitasking, 45 minutes

examples.label: Experience
examples.text: No talking about work until dessert

parts.name: Open and close with intention
parts.what: Don't open with logistics: prime guests beforehand and mark a threshold into the gathering. Don't end with thank-yous: give a last call, look inward at what happened, then turn outward toward ordinary life. [2,5,6]
how: Send a note beforehand that sets the mood [5]
End with a closing ritual, not an announcement [6]

examples.label: Physical
examples.text: A moment of silence before the meal

examples.label: Digital
examples.text: One word from everyone to close the call

examples.label: Experience
examples.text: A postcard mailed to guests a week later

framework.note: The book also describes **15 Toasts**, a dinner format where each guest gives a short, honest toast on a shared theme. [4]

system.name: The Gathering Design Canvas
system.intro: Plan any gathering in five passes, built from Parker's chapters.

steps.name: Purpose
steps.detail: Write it until someone could disagree with it. [2,3]

steps.name: People
steps.detail: Who serves the purpose, and who doesn't. [2]

steps.name: Rules
steps.detail: Two or three pop-up rules. [4]

steps.name: Threshold
steps.detail: How guests are primed and welcomed in. [5]

steps.name: Close
steps.detail: Last call, look inward, turn outward. [6]

example.title: A team offsite
items: **Purpose:** decide the one bet we make next year, not “team building”
**People:** the eight who own the decision
**Rules:** no laptops, no titles
**Threshold:** each person sends one question in advance
**Close:** everyone states the bet in their own words, then leaves together

reflect: Think of the last gathering you hosted. What was it really for?
Who did you invite out of habit rather than purpose?

steps: Pick an upcoming gathering: a dinner, a meeting, a celebration.
Write its category, then ask “why?” three times and rewrite the purpose until it's disputable.
Write two pop-up rules and a 30-second opening.
Design the ending: a last call and one shared moment of reflection.

books.inSedi: Plan the gathering as a project in Timely's Planning view, and put the event on the calendar with its purpose in the details.

books.title: Our Tribal Future
books.author: David R. Samson
books.about: *How to Channel Our Foundational Human Instincts into a Force for Good*: an evolutionary anthropologist argues that tribalism is a core human drive, and that we can direct it toward belonging and trust instead of division. [1,2]
books.authorBio: David R. Samson is an evolutionary anthropologist at the University of Toronto. The book won the 2023 Balsillie Prize for Public Policy. [3]

principle.name: Design for belonging, not against it
principle.body: Samson argues that we can't remove the urge to form tribes. It's an evolved drive that helped our ancestors survive, and he calls it the **Tribe Drive**. The question is where we point it: into small, real, trusting groups, or into abstract online camps that feed division. [1,4,5]

framework.name: From tribe drive to Team Human
framework.intro: Samson's main ideas, in the order the argument builds. These are his proposals; some are debated by other scholars. [4,6]

parts.name: The Tribe Drive
parts.what: Humans evolved to belong to nested groups, from family to band to tribe. The need is as basic as hunger. [1,6]
how: Notice which groups you actually draw identity and support from [5]

examples.label: Your day
examples.text: List the groups you'd say “we” about

examples.label: Your work
examples.text: Name the team you'd stay late for

examples.label: Your space
examples.text: The place where people know your name

parts.name: The Trust Paradox
parts.what: Our minds were built for kin and friends, yet we cooperate with millions of strangers. Samson describes trust growing in stages, from kin to friends to tribes held together by shared symbols. [4]
how: Use shared symbols and rituals to build trust between people who don't know each other yet [4]

examples.label: Your day
examples.text: A club shirt that starts conversations

examples.label: Your work
examples.text: Team rituals that welcome new people

examples.label: Your space
examples.text: A neighbourhood noticeboard

parts.name: Campcrafting
parts.what: Put social energy into small face-to-face groups modelled on the hunter-gatherer camp of about 20 to 30 people. Samson calls the practice of reducing distance between people **intentional proximity**. [4,6]
how: Create a recurring gathering for a small group, from a weekly brunch upward [4]

examples.label: Your day
examples.text: A standing weekly meal with the same friends

examples.label: Your work
examples.text: A small cross-team lunch group

examples.label: Your space
examples.text: Shared tools on the street

parts.name: Rituals and the meta-tribe
parts.what: Modern life, he argues, is under-ritualized. Rituals and symbols build trust. To protect against harmful tribalism he proposes **metabelief** (holding beliefs that change with evidence) and a shared identity he calls Team Human. [4,5]
how: Add a simple ritual to a group you care about [4]
Write down what evidence would change your mind on a belief you hold [4]

examples.label: Your day
examples.text: A toast to start every family dinner

examples.label: Your work
examples.text: “What would change our mind?” on every proposal

examples.label: Your space
examples.text: A yearly street party

framework.note: One academic reviewer, Joachim Krueger, questions some of the book's evolutionary claims and new terms. Read the ideas as Samson's proposals, not settled findings. [6]

system.name: Campcraft Your Circle
system.intro: Turn the book's ideas into a small, lasting group.

steps.name: Map your tribes
steps.detail: List the groups you belong to and mark each as face-to-face or abstract. [5]

steps.name: Shift your energy
steps.detail: Move time toward the face-to-face ones. [4,5]

steps.name: Gather a camp
steps.detail: Invite 4 to 10 people to a recurring meeting. [4]

steps.name: Give it a ritual
steps.detail: A name, a symbol or an opening ritual that's yours. [4]

steps.name: Check your beliefs
steps.detail: Practise metabelief together: what would change our minds? [4]

example.title: A neighbourhood supper club
items: **Map:** most of your “we” is online
**Shift:** one fewer evening scrolling each week
**Gather:** six neighbours, first Sunday of the month
**Ritual:** each host picks a song to open the meal
**Beliefs:** one friendly debate topic per dinner

reflect: Which of your tribes would show up for you in a hard week?
Where is your tribal instinct being used by someone else's algorithm?

steps: List the groups you're proud to belong to, and mark each face-to-face or abstract.
Pick 4 to 10 people for a small recurring gathering.
Give it a name or a simple opening ritual.
Hold it for eight weeks, then decide together whether to keep going.

books.title: The Psychology of Interpersonal Relations
books.author: Fritz Heider
books.about: A founding text of social psychology. Heider studied “naive psychology”: the common-sense theories everyone uses to explain why other people do what they do. [1,2]
books.authorBio: Fritz Heider (1896–1988) was an Austrian-born psychologist whose work on attribution and balance shaped modern social psychology. [2]

principle.name: Design for how people explain each other
principle.body: We constantly guess at the causes of other people's behavior, and those guesses shape how we treat them. Heider noticed we lean toward explaining others' actions by who they are rather than by the situation they're in. Later researchers named that tilt the fundamental attribution error. [2,3]

framework.name: Attribution and Balance
framework.intro: Two of Heider's ideas that are still used everywhere from design to diplomacy. [2]

parts.name: Attribution
parts.what: When someone acts, we explain it either by something inside them (traits, motives) or something outside (the circumstances). We tend to over-weight the inside explanation for others, especially when the behavior annoys us. [2,3]
how: Before judging, list situational reasons someone might act this way [2]

examples.label: Your day
examples.text: The driver who cut you off may be rushing to hospital

examples.label: Your work
examples.text: The late reply may come from an overloaded week, not disrespect

examples.label: Your space
examples.text: The messy kitchen may come from a broken dishwasher

parts.name: Balance
parts.what: People prefer their likes and dislikes to fit together: my friend's friend should be my friend, and if I like you and you like an idea, I'm pulled to like it too. An unbalanced triangle creates tension we try to resolve. [2]
how: When you feel tension in a relationship, map the triangle and see which link is out of balance [2]

examples.label: Your day
examples.text: A partner who loves a friend you find difficult

examples.label: Your work
examples.text: A manager you trust backing a plan you doubt

examples.label: Your space
examples.text: Housemates split over a shared rule

framework.note: Heider built on an earlier experiment with Marianne Simmel, in which people watching simple moving shapes described them as having intentions and personalities. [2,4]

system.name: The Charitable Explanation
system.intro: A short routine for moments of friction with someone.

steps.name: Write your first explanation
steps.detail: What do you think caused their behavior? [2]

steps.name: Flip it
steps.detail: Write three situational explanations instead. [2,3]

steps.name: Map the triangle
steps.detail: You, them and the issue: which link is negative? [2]

steps.name: Choose a response
steps.detail: Act on the most charitable explanation that's still plausible. [2]

steps.name: Check it
steps.detail: Ask, don't assume. [2]

example.title: A colleague who keeps missing deadlines
items: **First explanation:** they don't care
**Flip:** too many projects, unclear priorities, something at home
**Triangle:** you both care about the launch, but disagree about the timeline
**Response:** offer to agree on priorities together
**Check:** ask what's getting in the way

reflect: Whose behavior have you been explaining by their character rather than their circumstances?
Which relationship triangle in your life feels out of balance?

steps: Think of someone whose behavior bothers you.
Write your explanation, then three situational ones.
Draw the triangle of you, them and the issue, and mark each link + or −.
Decide on one conversation or one change of view.
